item.title: SALES: The Best Way to Eat Swiss Fondue? Floating on Lake Brienz
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
I could say that I was surprised to find myself and my family floating along in a red Zodiac on the deepest lake in Switzerland, eating cheese fondue and sipping white wine as the sun set. But really, it was all by design. When I designated myself as chief planner for an autumnal family trip to the Alpine nation with my adult children and their partners, I searched for an activity that would knock their socks off. I found it in Interlaken, with a floating fondue experience. Yes, you read that right. I love Switzerland, and have visited the land where the hills are alive with the sound of cowbells more than 30 times in my life. And while I’ve done many amazing things in and around the Swiss Alps—skiing, hiking, trottinetting, whittling my own Swiss cow from a block of wood—I knew getting my Gen Z crew excited about family time involved finding something a little more unconventional. We were going to be staying in the Bernese Oberland, a picture-postcard region with legendary sites like Grindelwald, the Jungfrau and Eiger mountains, and Interlaken. Everyone was up for hiking and taking cable cars to waterfalls; paragliding was sadly vetoed. But a unique culinary experience would surely work, I thought—the way to their hearts is through their stomachs. Luckily, I had heard about a Cheese Fondue Float experience offered by a company called Outdoor Switzerland a few years ago. Back then, it was raclette—toasted cheese scraped onto boiled potatoes—that served as the dish du jour. But fondue, Switzerland’s national dish, is much more well-known, so the company savvily swapped raclette trays for caquelons (ceramic fondue pots). I found the experience listing on Get Your Guide, and reviews praised the change, highlighting the delicious cheese and wine and the gregarious fondue fun. I confirmed a private booking for the six of us a month before we left home, and kept my fingers crossed for good weather. I needn’t have worried—my prayers were answered with glorious temperatures and bluebird skies on the day of the tour, a leisurely Sunday in September. A five-minute bus ride from downtown Interlaken brought us to the small village of Bonigen, the launch site located on scenic Lake Brienz. After shaking hands with our guide, a tall, friendly Dutchman named Hild, we donned life jackets, listened to the mandatory safety briefing, and stepped into the boat, alternating sides to keep the weight even. Once comfortably settled around the pretty red-and-white-checkered tablecloth, which was already topped with plates, cups, and two fondue pots, Hild slowly rowed us onto the lake. Lake Brienz is the deepest lake in the country, and it’s surely one of the most scenic too. Moving out from the shore, we encountered spectacular views of towering mountains, their peaks mirrored in the impossibly blue water. I poured the prepared cheese fondue into the heated fondue pots, and the mixture began bubbling, filling the air with a sharp aroma as it warmed into readiness. The fondue float experience includes white wine (one 500-ml bottle per person), as well as water and hot tea. We took turns pouring wine into our copper cups as my eldest son took command of the Bluetooth speaker, setting a lively mood with traditional Alpine tunes played on accordions and hackbretts (a kind of dulcimer), mixed with the occasional yodel ditty. At one point, our float’s music and laughter brought friendly waves from passengers on a passing cruise boat, along with toots from the ship’s horn. We whooped and waved in return. Once the cheese was steaming hot, we dipped and swished bread cubes into the melted goodness, savoring the delicious alchemy of bread and cheese alongside celebratory toasts in honor of our family adventure. As the cheese disappeared, the fondue pot heated the remains into what the Swiss call “la réligieuse”—toasted cheese bits that are scraped from the bottom of the pot. We fought playfully over dibs on the last delicious morsels—trust me, they’re good to the last perfectly browned crumb. The entire experience lasted about an hour and a half, and during that time, the six of us managed to drink all six wine bottles on board. None of us are big drinkers, but the beauty of the surroundings inspired the good times to flow, and, well, so did the wine. Photos and videos captured our cheesy adventure, but the memory of enjoying such a unique culinary and cultural experience with my favorite people in the world will be forever burned into my mind. You can have a fondue anywhere, but while floating in one of the most iconic locations in one of the most beautiful countries on earth? Even my discerning Gen Z travel companions agreed: “That’s extra.” The Cheese Fondue Float experience on Lake Brienz in Interlaken is available to book on the Outdoor Switzerland website, as well as on GetYourGuide and Viator. It is offered between September and April, weather permitting. If booking in the colder months, bundle up with coats, beanies, and gloves, as you’ll be out on the water for up to an hour and a half. Private charters are available for groups up to eight people; kids eight years and up are welcome. More of a dessert person? Outdoor Switzerland also offers a Swiss Chocolate Fondue experience. Get cozy under blankets, sip hot tea, and dip marshmallows and fruit into creamy melted Swiss chocolate while a qualified guide rows you merrily along the beautiful Brienzersee.

item.title: REVIEW: Creative XF1 review: although not truly perfect, these active desktop speakers get pretty close for not a lot of money
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
The Creative XF1 is without doubt one of the smartest, most cost-effective ways of turning your desktop into a venue for high-quality, hi-res audio. It’s not the complete solution, but it gets a fair way towards it — and it’s absolutely ideal for those who want to feel like they’re having plenty of input into the sound they’re experiencing - +Usefully compact dimensions and almost-as-useful cork stands - +Control app offers a lot of input into the performance - -Low frequencies are lumpy and rather one-note - -Difficult to achieve a truly uncoloured sound - -Crying out for more options where finish is concerned Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. For a cent short of $180 (or a penny short of £140) Creative will sell you its XF1 desktop stereo speaker system — and don’t imagine this money buys anything less than a fully featured and serious product. It may look a little frivolous, especially when its cork ‘wedge’ stands are attached, but the XF1 is all business. And besides, those stands elevate the speakers to the point they’re firing at your ears rather than your torso. An active and bi-amped arrangement that requires the speakers to be wired together and one of them to be connected to mains power, the Creative XF1 has a total of 72 watts of power on board — ample in the context of the most likely use cases. Bluetooth connectivity is on board, too with codec compatibility including the high-end LDAC option, and the USB-C input on the rear of the main speaker allows for genuinely hi-res content to be an option. There’s also an analog socket for additional input flexibility. Very acceptable specification is complemented by a more-than-adequate standard of build and finish, a couple of colour options (black or white, monochrome fans) and a control app that features a 10-band PEQ offering an enormous amount of end-user input into the eventual sound. And that sound has plenty going for it. Good enough for our best stereo speakers guide? For this sort of money, absolutely. There’s not a huge amount of variation at the bottom end, it’s true, and not a whole lot of momentum either, but elsewhere the XF1 does good work. Detail retrieval is impressive, the simple scale of sound it’s capable of generating is almost startling, and there’s a real facility for midrange communication. Add in a fair amount of dynamic headroom, as well as a proper sensation of focus and separation even if you’re sitting very close to the speakers, and it should be apparent that a place on your shortlist is the very least the Creative XF1 deserves. Creative XF1 Review: Price and release date The Creative XF1 desktop stereo speaker system is on sale now, and in the United Kingdom it will cost you £139. It goes for $179 in the United States, while in Australia it sells for AU$339. Usually, we wax lyrical about competing products at the level, but to do that here I'd likely need to delve into cheaper Bluetooth solo speaker options, bought twice and put in stereo mode. Even Ruark's Mk1 line (now into its third iteration) bijou stereo speakers are more than twice the price. Know this: this is not a lot of money for such a proposition. Very few companies will give you more for less, although Logitech, with its Z407 is one notable example that can be yours for just a touch less than the Creative. Keep both the modest nature of the asking price and the equally modest physical dimensions of the XF1 uppermost in your mind and it's difficult not to be at least a little impressed by the way it’s specified. There’s no facility to swap the orientation of the speakers — the one that takes care of connectivity and needs mains power is the right channel and that’s an end of it. Here’s where you plug in your sources using either USB-C (the XF1 can natively handle digital audio files of up to 24bit/96kHz resolution) or line-level analogue 3.5mm inputs on the rear of the speaker, and where you connect to the left channel using a supplied four-pin cable. There’s also a pre-out for a subwoofer, an ‘energy saving’ switch that will power down an inactive XF1 if you set it to the ‘on’ position, and a button to initiate Bluetooth pairing. Wireless connectivity is on board the right speaker, too — the Creative uses Bluetooth 6.0, and is compatible with LDAC as well as the more common SBC and AAC codecs. That four-pin cable carries all audio data from right to left, and all power requirements too. Creative has specified a block of Class D amplification for each of the drivers in the XF1 — each 19mm soft-dome tweeter gets 10 watts of power, and each 76mm mid/bass driver (designed using what Creative describes as ‘finite element analysis’ for minimal distortion) gets 26 watts to play with. An all-in total of 72 watts should really prove ample in a system that’s almost certain to be no kind of meaningful distance from your ears when it’s in position — especially when you factor in the back-firing bass reflex port towards the top of the rear of each cabinet. Creative suggests frequency response from this arrangement is 55Hz - 40kHz. - Manages to sound spacious yet focused at the same time - Slightly plodding character to the low end If you’re using the XF1 on a desktop, the chances are you won’t need to explore the outer reaches of its abilities where volume is concerned. If you’re sitting a greater distance from them, though, never worry that these little cabinets will sound lost. They’re louder than they look. And no matter the volume level at which you’re listening, the Creative system sounds bigger than it looks, too. A 24bit/44.1kHz FLAC file of Lorde’s Shapeshifter sounds open and spacious, with plenty of air around the elements of the recording — but at the same time the speakers manage to focus the performance quite convincingly too. There’s a commonality to the way it presents the recording, a togetherness that’s by no means a given in systems like this, especially not systems that cost as relatively little as this. The idea of a soundstage is made more than just a notion. With the qualified exception of the bottom of the frequency range, the XF1 does good work in identifying details in a recording and giving them the sort of context and weighting they require. It’s particularly adept in the midrange, where the smallest variations in tone or timbre or texture are picked up on — it serves to make voices sound characterful and individualistic. The tonal balance is never truly neutral no matter how you might finesse the PEQ settings, but the suggestion of heat does at least serve to mitigate the tweeter’s tendency to hit the highest frequencies with rather too much enthusiasm. There’s a reasonable amount of dynamic headroom available, so if your music (or your movie, or your game) ticks off a big up- or downshift in volume or intensity, the XF1 doesn’t panic. It maintains its composure and its tonal balance, its frequency response doesn’t alter, and it does a reasonable job of putting meaningful distance between the most and least attacking sounds. At the bottom of the frequency range the Creative is a little less assured and a little less successful. It hits admirably hard, but bass isn’t as well controlled as the rest of the frequency information, and can plod a little as a result — this has an unwelcome knock-on effect where rhythmic expression is concerned. And the low end is all rather one-note - there’s little of the variation or the fine detail available here that’s apparent elsewhere. Switch to Bluetooth stream of Girl and Girl’s Call a Doctor and, broadly speaking, the XF1 maintains its attitude and fundamental character. Derail levels drop away just a fraction, and there’s a little less positivity where stereo focus and separation are concerned, but taken as a whole the Creative is a perfectly viable system where wireless music is concerned. - 191 x 100 x 155mm (HxWxD) Desktop space is usually at a premium, of course, so the XF1’s 191 x 100 x 155mm (HxWxD) dimensions are usefully compact. And given that most desktops are lower than the ears of the person who’s sitting at it, the appearance of a couple of detachable cork stands that raise each speaker at an angle of 15° is very welcome indeed. The speakers themselves are made almost entirely from MDF, and from the curves along each horizontal edge to the slightly soft-touch matte finish, they look a little more expensive than they actually are — and this is true no matter if you've chosen the white finish or the black of my sample. The standard of build and finish wouldn’t disgrace a system costing two or three times this amount. Creative XF1 review: Usability and setup - One physical control plus an LED tell-take - ‘Wireless’ means a minimum of two wires As far as setting up the XF1 is concerned, there’s really not much to it. As with most ‘wireless’ speaker systems, some wires are necessary — in this instance, there’s a wire from the right speaker to the left carrying all power and data, and another from the right speaker to a mains power supply. Make these two connections, pair a smartphone via Bluetooth and you’re good to go - or you may decide to go the whole hi-res hog and make a USB-C connection from a laptop or smartphone with a premium music streaming service on board. There’s a single turn/push control dial on the front baffle of the right speaker, along with a tell-tale LED- here’s where you get control of power on/off, volume and input selection. And there’s also the Creative Nexus control app — it features precisely no playback controls, but it does allow you to check on firmware updates and let the system know if it’s on a desktop or not. It also gives access to a 10-band PEQ that has scope for custom settings as well as literally dozens upon dozens of presets, some of Creative’s own design, some uploaded by users. As with most Creative systems, the sensation of value for money is pretty strong with the XF1. Sonically it’s not without its issues, as I’ve discussed — but it’s possible to weigh these against the things it gets right in audio terms, the standard of the build and finish that’s on display, the neat and tidy dimensions, and the amount of tweaking the PEQ allows and still conclude you’re getting your money’s-worth. Should I buy the Creative XF1? Buy it if... Use the system’s USB-C input and access to a native 24bit/96kHz DAC is yours. Creative supplies cork stands for the XF1 but you have to screw them into place yourself. You want your sound to be bigger than your speakers Considering their compact dimensions, the Creative generate impressive sonic scale. Don't buy it if... In that case you’re going to need something battery-powered. The XF1 isn’t the most sonically coloured system around, but it has a flavour of its own. The Creative can sound a little lumpy and unchanging at the bottom end - there’s admirable weight but not all that much subtlety. Spending less money with Logitech buys you more stuff — and on a pound-for-pound basis the Logitech Z407 makes a lot of sense. The inclusion of a subwoofer means genuine low-frequency presence and control is available, and the super-compact speakers will fit more-or-less anywhere. Not quite the poise or the overall balance of the XF1, and not the ease of operation either — but a profoundly competitive proposition nonetheless. Read our full Logitech Z407 review. Naturally I position the Creative XF1 on my desktop, a speaker on either side of my MacBook Pro. Plugged into the mains, connected to each other and with a USB-C cable running from the laptop to the rear on the right speaker, I am able to access lots of hi-res content via the Qobuz and TIDAL apps. I also connect an iPhone 15 Pro and a FiiO M15S digital audio player wirelessly via Bluetooth — the latter allows use of the LDAC codec, and connecting it via its 3.5mm headphone output to the Creative’s corresponding input allows me to assess how effective (or otherwise) the XF1’s digital-to-analogue conversion is.

item.title: REVIEW: These 3 community plugins fix Obsidian’s most annoying missing features
item.description:
Source: How-To Geek
Obsidian is, in my opinion, incredibly powerful because it keeps its core feature set intentionally lean. It’s designed to be customizable, and the community plugins are what fill those gaps. But sometimes, those plugins don't just add cool features—they fix fundamental problems that, honestly, feel like things the app should have out of the box. Here are the three best plugins I've found, in no particular order. You can look them all up on Obsidian's internal plugin searcher, so you don't need to look for anything external here. Smaller files, cleaner names, and editing without leaving Obsidian Obsidian treats images almost like an afterthought. It’s a pain point that every note-taker runs into. You paste a screenshot, and the app drops the raw file into your vault with a generic, timestamped name like “Pasted image.” It doesn't care about format or resolution. Do this a hundred times, and your vault quietly swells with unnecessary megabytes—especially painful if you’re syncing across devices or using Git. Image Converter, built by xRyul, intercepts images the moment they enter the vault, solving this mess immediately. You can convert pasted or dropped files to WEBP, JPG, or PNG, and it handles compression and resizing automatically. A huge, bulky PNG screenshot can end up in your notes at a fraction of its original size, zero manual work required. Bonus: it supports HEIC (the default iPhone image format), which Obsidian struggles to display natively depending on your operating system's built-in codec support. But it does much more than just shrink files. You can resize images simply by dragging their corners, or using a modifier key and the scroll wheel—and it writes those perfect dimensions right into the link. The built-in annotation tool means you no longer need external editors just to draw on or mark up a diagram. Plus, it lets you rename attachments using custom rules with variables, ensuring every file lands in your vault in a predictable way. Need a quick copy? The right-click menu adds immediate actions, like copying the image or deleting it from the vault alongside its link. Cool stuff, right? That last option is the clincher. Managing attachments is a basic requirement for any modern note-taking app, and Obsidian’s current handling stops right at "save the file." Image Converter has attracted over 400,000 downloads and functions perfectly on both desktop and mobile. The one problem: it doesn't really work on phones. But it's neat for the desktop version. Relevant search that reaches deep into PDFs and images Obsidian’s built-in search is technically impressive. It supports operators, regex, and scoped queries like path: and tag:, which is fantastic if you know exactly what you're looking for. But most of us don't start that way. We remember a vague phrase, a partially spelled word, or just the general idea of a note, and the core search engine rarely returns the most relevant result first. Omnisearch, created by Simon Cambier, takes a radically different approach to this. It's designed to be the search engine that just works, in a way. Using the BM25 scoring algorithm under the hood, it intelligently ranks results by relevance. It tolerates typos, prioritizes matches found in titles and headings over text buried in the body, and truly surfaces the note you meant, instead of just listing every note that happens to contain a random keyword. It feels less like a text filter and more like a Google search. Its biggest game-changer? Files that aren't Markdown. Paired with its companion plugin, Text Extractor, Omnisearch indexes PDFs, Office documents, and even images. It runs OCR, meaning text inside scanned pages or lecture slides instantly becomes searchable. For students and researchers managing massive vaults of PDFs and photos, this turns a pile of attachments into actionable, findable knowledge. Users have spoken: Omnisearch boasts over 1.3 million downloads and was recognized in Obsidian’s Gems of the Year awards. A note-taking app is only as valuable as its ability to retrieve what you’ve written. When a third-party plugin consistently outperforms the native tool, that feature belongs in the core experience. The ability to rename and merge tags across your entire vault Renaming a note in Obsidian is pure magic. The app updates every link pointing to it across your vault, and you never have to think about it. But tags? They get no such treatment. If you decide that #ml should actually be #machine-learning the core app offers zero way to rename that tag everywhere at once. This request has been running on the Obsidian forum for years, and the consensus answer from power users is simple: install Tag Wrangler. Tag Wrangler, by PJ Eby, adds powerful controls to the Tags view, allowing you to rename, merge, toggle, and search tags globally. Renaming isn't a blind find-and-replace; it uses Obsidian’s own parse data to locate genuine tags, ensuring your change never accidentally affects text that just looks like a tag. Even hierarchical tags behave intelligently: renaming a parent like #project automatically renames all its child tags. Merging tags is risky, as you might imagine, and the plugin handles this by asking for confirmation and warning you that the change is permanent. It’s sophisticated enough to handle these edge cases. And it keeps improving: newer versions add dedicated tag pages, making tags more robust. Even with some technical gaps (like certain newer database views), the plugin has nearly a million downloads and fills a structural gap in the core app that has persisted far too long. All three of these solve some of the most common and frustrating problems every Obsidian user eventually hits. And until Obsidian builds these core capabilities in, I firmly believe that all three are must-installs on day one.

item.title: REVIEW: The pros and cons of using an Amazfit smartwatch
item.description:
Source: Engadget
The pros and cons of using an Amazfit smartwatch Amazfit watches are easy on your wallet, but they can’t do everything. We may receive a commission on purchases made from links. Amazfit smartwatches are widely considered to be good alternatives to the bigger brands. They're generally cheaper, with some models like the well-reviewed Amazfit Bip 6 available for as little as $80. But as you would expect, there are concessions to be made to justify the lower price. The line from the Chinese company Zepp Health includes a wide range of smartwatches to suit any lifestyle, from casual wearers to serious athletes. However, they run on a proprietary OS that limits app access, and some models have limited storage. The companion app also isn't the most intuitive. On the plus side, Amazfit smartwatches focus on AI-powered software using its Zepp Coach and offer long battery life, with some models lasting for up to 25 days per charge. You can also find deals on Amazfit smartwatches, which are already affordable to begin with. Before you commit, it helps to know what you're getting and what you're giving up. Here's why so many people consider Amazfit in the first place. Why Amazfit smartwatches are worth considering Amazfit smartwatches are sleek, with designs that resemble other popular models. You'll find square-shaped options like the Bip 6 and Active 2 (Square) that look like an Apple Watch. There are also round-faced ones like the Amazfit Active Max and the Amazfit T-Rex 3, which is designed for outdoor adventurers and resembles a Garmin watch in its aesthetic. Another advantage is cross-device compatibility. You can pair an Amazfit smartwatch with either iPhone or Android since it uses its own operating system and isn't tied to either. Many trusted outlets also rank Amazfit watch models among the best budget smartwatches, citing accurate health tracking along with their stylish designs. They also note that integrations like the AI Coach, Bluetooth calling and Alexa command support are top-notch. Amazfit smartwatches also offer over 100 sports modes, from strength training and running to gardening and Tai Chi. And they have all the important sensors you'd want for data, including heart rate, sleep, temperature, GPS and more. Amazfit is a solid budget smartwatch brand you can continue to use even if you swap phone platforms. There's also no subscription tier for any of the data it tracks and reports, and these watches are a step up from the best cheap fitness trackers, with larger screens for at-a-glance information and control on your wrist. Amazfit smartwatches are not without downsides Amazfit smartwatches run on the proprietary Zepp OS, so you can't access third-party apps the way you can with Wear OS watches. Instead, you're limited to a few productivity apps and games from the Zepp Store. The watches do integrate with third-party platforms like Strava, TrainingPeaks, Komoot and Runna, but you can't access Google Wallet, Google Maps, Uber, Starbucks, Gmail or banking apps. There's no Spotify app either, though you can listen on your phone and use the watch to control playback or use a remote app to mirror Spotify on the device. Beyond apps, the software isn't as intuitive as others or as easy to navigate as those of better-known brands. You'll see unfamiliar terms like PAI, Amazfit's personal activity score and Biocharge, which is basically its equivalent of a readiness score. Some models have limited storage, which could cause issues with storing workout data or apps. The Amazfit Bip 6, for example, has 512MB of storage. On longevity, Amazfit offers only three years of software and security support for its smartwatches. They won't stop working after that point, but it's worth factoring into the decision if you plan to hold onto the smartwatch for a while. For a more intuitive experience with better app support, you might prefer going with affordable models from brands like Fitbit and Garmin instead, or even an older-model Samsung Galaxy Watch or Apple Watch, even if they're in their last years of software support. While Amazfit smartwatches aren't the best smartwatches you can buy, you will get reliable health tracking, long battery life and sleek designs for a great price, with a few caveats you might be able to live with.

item.title: REVIEW: Asus ZenScreen OLED MQ16FC Review: Affordable OLED Hits the Road
item.description:
Source: PCMag
The Asus ZenScreen OLED MQ16FC ($279) is among the most reasonably priced OLED portable monitors available today. Sleek and lightweight, this portable display is a fine choice as a secondary monitor for creative types and frequent travelers—indeed, for anyone who wants to experience the benefits of OLED at just a modest premium over comparable IPS panels. It foregoes UHD (4K) resolution, which keeps its price down while still rendering sharp, colorful still and video images on its 16-inch screen. It earns our Editors' Choice award as a mainstream 16-inch portable monitor with a high-quality screen. The MQ16FC, clad in a handsome aluminum frame, measures 9.2 by 14.2 by 0.4 inches and weighs just 1.5 pounds. It houses a 16-inch (measured diagonally) OLED screen with WUXGA (1,920-by-1,200-pixel) native resolution and a 16:10 aspect ratio, which provides extra vertical real estate compared with a widescreen format. Some creators may hesitate to buy the MQ16FC because of its modest native resolution, but its screen still offers a relatively high pixel density of 142 pixels per inch (ppi) given its size. That's good enough for most creative work, if well short of panels such as Apple's Retina displays, which have pixel densities exceeding 200ppi. The MQ16FC's pixel density is effectively the same as the ViewSonic ColorPro VP16-OLED, an Editors' Choice portable monitor for creatives, as well as the Ricoh Portable Monitor BW150. The Asus ZenScreen Duo OLED (MQ149CD) stacks a pair of 14-inch WUXGA OLED panels with a healthy pixel density (161ppi), but it sells for $599. Portable displays with 4K UHD OLED screens are rare, and most come from little-known brands. An exception is the 15.6-inch ViewSonic VX1655-4K-OLED, which sports a screen with Retina-level pixel density (282 ppi), but it is nearly twice the price of the MQ16FC. The MQ16FC's aluminum chassis is supported by a fold-out kickstand that allows you to fine-tune the panel's tilt angle. Also on the back is a hole with a quarter-inch thread to fit a tripod. The monitor comes with a padded cloth case to protect it when you're storing it or traveling. The MQ16FC has two USB-C ports that support DisplayPort Alt Mode and up to 65 watts of power delivery. When you plug the monitor into an outlet using the included power adapter, it can power or charge a laptop connected to it; when it's unplugged, you can draw power from its host computer over a USB-C connection. You'll also find a mini HDMI port; the monitor includes a mini HDMI-to-HDMI cable and a USB-C-to-USB-C cable. These ports are on the monitor's right-hand edge, along with a power button, a scroll wheel for working the on-screen display (OSD), and a headphone jack. (The MQ16FC lacks built-in speakers.) We did our color and brightness testing using a Klein K10-A colorimeter and Portrait Displays' CalMAN Ultimate 2026 software. Asus rates the MQ16FC's luminance at 300 nits (candelas per square meter); in our testing, it measured 262 nits in SDR mode and 283 nits in HDR. This should be fine for indoor use in rooms with modest ambient light. OLED monitors generally have relatively low overall brightness compared with other technologies, to prevent burn-in and overheating. (Rather than being backlit, each pixel generates its own light in response to an electrical current.) These monitors' spectacular contrast and vivid colors mitigate the need for high brightness. Asus rates the MQ16FC's typical contrast ratio at 100,000:1; we measured it at 81,363:1. This is far greater than what we see from in-plane switching (IPS) panels, which typically have contrast ratios of about 1,000:1. Screens using the IPS Black variant have contrast ratios up to 3,000:1, and vertical alignment (VA) panels up to 5,000:1. OLED panels have such phenomenal contrast, highlighted by deep black tones, because they have the ability to turn individual pixels, or groups of pixels, off and on. (Theoretically, OLED screens should have infinite contrast ratios, as contrast ratio represents the brightness ratio between the brightest whites and deepest blacks.) Suffice it to say that the MQ16FC's contrast is impressive. Asus rates the MQ16FC's DCI-P3 color coverage at 95%. In our testing, it had effectively complete (99.65%) coverage of DCI-P3, a color space geared to digital video, as shown in the chromaticity (color quality and coverage) chart below. The squares represent target color reference points, and the circles represent the actual measured color. In the Adobe RGB space, which is primarily used for preparing art for print, the MQ16FC did nearly as well, achieving 97.64% coverage. For sRGB, the universal color standard for websites and web-based art, it covered 145% of the space by area (see the chromaticity chart below). Coverage greater than 100% produces rich, vivid colors, though it risks oversaturation. Asus does not provide coverage figures for either Adobe RGB or sRGB. We also benchmarked the MQ16FC's Delta E (dE), a measure of color accuracy, namely the difference between the hue of a displayed color and the color input that the monitor received. The dE figure that appears in monitor specs is the average of many individual color readings across the spectrum; the lower the value, the more accurate the color. Asus rates the MQ16FC's average dE at below 2, which indicates color accurate enough that a casual observer may be unable to distinguish any variation between the color on screen and the intended (source) color. We tested its dE out of the box at 3.17, not as good as its rating but decent as far as monitors go. To ensure the most accurate colors, creators who buy this panel may want to calibrate it themselves using a Datacolor Spyder, X-Rite, or Klein colorimeter, and software such as Calman or DisplayCAL. In my ad hoc experiential testing, in which I viewed images from our photo test suite and selected movie clips, the MQ16FC rendered both still and video images well. Photos and scenes looked reasonably bright, with vivid colors and excellent retention of detail in bright and dark areas—in short, the quality we have come to expect from big-screen OLED panels, but in a portable display costing less than $300. - 5.0 - Exemplary: Near perfection, ground-breaking - 4.5 - Outstanding: Best in class, acts as a benchmark for measuring competitors - 4.0 - Excellent: A performance, feature, or value leader in its class, with few shortfalls - 3.5 - Good: Does what the product should do, and does so better than many competitors - 3.0 - Average: Does what the product should do, and sits in the middle of the pack - 2.5 - Fair: We have some reservations, buy with caution - 2.0 - Subpar: We do not recommend, buy with extreme caution - 1.0 - Dismal: Don't even think about buying this product Read Our Editorial Mission Statement and Testing Methodologies. OLED monitor ownership is no longer restricted to those with deep pockets; displays using this technology have come down in price to the point that they often cost little more than their IPS counterparts. Leading this egalitarian charge are portable monitors, which tend to be modestly priced to begin with. The Asus ZenScreen OLED MQ16FC lists at $279.99 and is often generously discounted. It lacks the UHD (4K) resolution of some other portable OLED displays, but it comes in at a lower price, and on a 16-inch screen its pixel density is still high enough for photo and video editing. Whether you're a creator looking for a secondary screen, a business traveler wanting to add some color to your presentations and sizzle reels, or a gamer or movie buff wanting to display your entertainment in its best light, with the MQ16FC the promise of OLED can be yours for less than $300. It earns our Editors' Choice nod as the best mainstream 16-inch portable display you can buy. I currently focus my efforts on 3D printers, pro and productivity displays, and drives and SSDs of all sorts. Over the years, I have reviewed smart telescopes, iPad and iPhone science apps, plus the occasional camera, laptop, keyboard, and mouse. I've also written a host of articles about astronomy, space science, travel photography, and astrophotography for PCMag and its past and present sibling publications (among them, Mashable and ExtremeTech), as well as for the former PCMag Digital Edition.

item.title: REVIEW: Shark PowerDetect Transformer review: a strong, versatile vac that switches from upright to stick
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
The flexible 3-in-1 transforming design that allows you to easily switch between upright, stick and handheld vacuum might be the Shark PowerDetect Transformer’s most attention-grabbing feature. But what really impressed me is its strong suction and super-smart auto-detection — it adapts to different flooring, edges and quantities of dirt automatically, making sucking up dust, debris and even pet hair a breeze. Couple in how easy it is to empty and it’s an impressive vacuum that should make handling your whole home easy. - +Packed with smart auto-detection features Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. Shark PowerDetect Transformer: two-minute review The Shark PowerDetect Transformer is a wired vacuum cleaner that combines an upright, stick and handheld vacuum all in one. It offers plenty of the premium features you might expect, including tangle-free brush bar and dirt-illuminating LED, but also comes crammed with smart features like automatic dirt, surface and edge detection. The Shark PowerDetect Transformer admittedly isn’t the most easily wielded vacuum cleaner in its upright form — weighing in at 17.6 lbs / 8kg — but it has a trick up its sleeve. Press a single button and its vacuum pod pops off, turning it into a svelte stick vacuum with its own discrete dust bin. Need even more flexibility? Pop off the top section and it becomes a handy handheld vac. Switching between each system is seriously swift, which is really smart design. On top of this, the PowerDetect Transformer also offers an excellent range of accessories for different tasks, so you’re not just limited to its talented DuoClean Detect nozzle. The HairPro Self-Cleaning Pet Power brush is great for getting pet hair off your rugs and furniture — with its anti-tangle tech preventing the bar getting clogged — and it also includes old classics like a crevice tool and a multi-surface brush. On top of this, it has built-in HEPA certified filtration and an anti-allergen seal, which the asthma sufferers in my house definitely appreciate. In my book though, the thing that helps the PowerDetect Transformer rival the best vacuum cleaners is how hassle-free it makes sucking up crud from your carpets and hard flooring. Absolutely chock full of auto-detection features, it will dial the level of its suction up and down depending on your floor type, the amount of dirt it detects or the direction you’re dragging it in. Even smarter is its edge detection, which senses when you’re vacuuming against furniture and along room boundaries and directs its suction toward them to more completely do away with detritus. I’ll admit that being smart doesn’t necessarily always translate being capable. Fortunately, all these smarts do make Shark’s vacuum seriously good at shifting dirt. Pretty much every test I put the PowerDetect Transformer through it aced, getting up coarse dirt from a hard floor and dust out of a shallow pile carpet in a single sweep. And when vacuuming room edges — the achilles heel of many vacuum cleaners — every single lentil I’d tossed down vanished in one movement. The fact pretty much all of this happened without me having to tap a single button is just the icing on the cake. On top of this, its brush bars were able to remove a disturbing quantity of cat hair from my upholstery without getting clogged, making it easy to clean up after my champion shedder. However, while the bars themselves were great at avoiding tangles, I did find that a couple of times a snarl of hair got caught around the exit into the cyclone chamber, causing it to get slightly backed up. This only happened a few times and won’t matter much as long as you empty the vacuum often enough to stop the hose getting backed up, but it’s worth bearing in mind for the hairiest households. Once you’re finished, emptying the Shark is also seriously straightforward. After using either its handheld or stick modes, clipping its vacuum pod back on triggers its self-emptying cycle, rapidly emptying its smaller dust bin. And when you want to empty the vacuum pod itself, all you have to do is press the bin switch to detach the larger bin, hold it over your bin and unhook a catch to open the bottom and jettison its contents. Perhaps the one criticism I do have of the PowerDetect Transformer’s performance is it’s very loud — measuring it with a sound level meter, it hit 74dB during upright use and a raucous 82dB during its self-cleaning cycle. So if you have sensitive neighbors or, like mine, your cat tends toward the scaredy, it might not be the one for you. Still though, all in all, the Shark PowerDetect Transformer is an impressive vacuum cleaner. Not only is it powerful, it’s smart, easy to use and flexible enough to vacuum pretty much every area of your home. Yes, wireless is always a nice to have — although its 8m cable meant I didn’t miss this as much as I thought I would — it’s loud and it occasionally gets a bit backed up. But I’m happy to forgive these minor quibbles given how much easier it makes day-to-day cleaning. Shark PowerDetect Transformer review: price & availability Having launched on June 30, 2026, the Shark PowerDetect Transformer is widely available now. It goes for a list price of $529.99 / £499.99 / AU$699.99 — although at the time of writing, in the US, you can use the code TRIO at the checkout to save $130, bringing it down to $399.99. That price is hardly chicken feed but, for what you’re getting, it’s still reasonable value. For example, the Shark PowerDetect Cordless — our current pick for the best vacuum cleaner out there — is priced at a roughly equivalent $429.99 / £499.99 / AU$849.99 and while unlike the Transformer it’s fully wireless, it can’t convert into a full, high-capacity upright. Meanwhile, the premium Dyson Gen5detect is much more spendy at $949.99 / £769.99 / AU$1,549, while rocking relatively similar features. In return for your spend, you’re not only getting three vacuums in one but also a solid range of accessories. It comes with the classics such as brush and crevice tools but it also packs a stair tool, the HairPro Pet Power Brush for powered action against pet fuzz and an anti-allergen dusting brush. It also comes with a handy accessory bag to keep them all in. Finally, the Shark PowerDetect Transformer comes in two tasty colorways: Chimera Blue — a dusky sky blue — and Deep Sage Green. Both of these really pop, especially with those gold highlights, although I’d say I just marginally prefer the former. Shark PowerDetect Transformer review: specs Shark PowerDetect Transformer review: design Okay, I’ll admit when I first heard the name Shark Transformer, I was hoping I was going to be getting a toy robot that converted into a toothy, predatory fish. Fortunately, the design of this vacuum cleaner is nearly as cool. Its modular design makes it easy to switch between three different modes — heavy-duty upright vacuum cleaner, lightweight stick vac and flexible handheld — at the click of a button. Moreover, unlike previous 3-in-1 vacuum cleaners Shark has created, this one is a hoseless design, meaning you don’t have to hook and unhook elephant trunk tubing every time you want to switch modes. Sliding the vacuum pod on and off the wand, it just clicks into place and connects to the vacuum’s airlock in one smooth movement. It’s clever design and makes selecting the right tool for your job feel effortless. Naturally, as a result of this protean form, it’s quite hard to comment on the overall size and weight of the device. Because in its upright vacuum final evolution it’s a pretty bulky and hefty beast but pop off a couple of sections and suddenly you’re left with something super light and flexible. So it’s a bit of a quantum vacuum cleaner: a superposition of heavy and light at the same time. Fortunately, when it comes to its appearance, the PowerDetect Transformer is far less paradoxical. I’m definitely picking up what Shark is throwing down here: in its stick and handheld modes, the Transformer looks seriously sleek and although the vacuum pod is pretty hulking, it’s still excellently engineered. On top of this, the colorways on offer are stunning — the deep sage green colorway I tested looks great but the chimera blue version is genuinely droolworthy. Genuinely, it gives me the same vibes as my sky blue MacBook Air and I wants it. Setting the Shark up for the first time is pretty straightforward, even if compared to other wired vacuums there is some assembly required. Essentially, all you need to do is click the wand into place on the nozzle, slide the vacuum pod into its home on the stick and insert the hand vacuum into the top. After this, you’re basically all set to start sucking up grit right away, because the Transformer neither has smart home features to set up or battery to charge. And don’t sweat this last omission too much — its eight-meter cable means you should be able to comfortably reach most areas of your home. Alongside all of these modules, the Transformer also features all of the usual suspects in terms of accessories, such as the brush and the crevice tool. However, it doesn’t stop there: it also includes Shark’s HairPro Self-Cleaning Pet Power brush, a miniature brush bar tool with anti-wrap technology for getting pet hair and dander out from carpets and upholstery. But by far its smartest tool is its DuoClean Detect nozzle. On top of its self-cleaning brush roll that picks up hair without getting tangled and targeted LED lighting for showing up barely visible specs of dirt, it’s also absolutely crammed with smart auto-detection features. Whether it’s sensing your floor type, adjusting to the quantity of dirt, directing suction forward or backward depending on the direction you’re moving in or automatically targeting its air inflow to gulp down detritus right up to the edge of rooms, it does all the hard work so you can just focus on practicing your Freddie Mercury impression. Given all of these auto-detection features, the controls on the Shark PowerDetect Transformer are almost comically uncomplicated. There’s an on button… and that’s basically all you need to understand. If you’re a real control freak, you can manually set its suction to match hard floor, shallow pile or deep pile carpet but honestly I never needed to manually control this, as its auto-detect features did a perfectly effective job at dialing its suction up and down. Finally, given I live with someone who both suffers from asthma and has the nasal sensitivity of a sommelier with a Neti pot, I definitely appreciate how the Transformer handles dust and disagreeable odors. Its HEPA-certified filtration and anti-allergen seal keeps all of that bronchial-irritating crud locked away. And once you’ve popped one of Shark’s odor-neutralizing cartridges into the nozzle, you can dial its stench-scrubbing capabilities up or down to remove any distressing scents the grime kicks up. Shark PowerDetect Transformer review: performance - Fantastic suction in almost every scenario Given how clever its features are, this vacuum cleaner is clearly a real bright shark. But how does that translate into real-world performance? After all, what good is the cold, calculating mind of a great white if it’s stuck in the ungainly body of a sunfish? Fortunately, you don’t need to worry on this front — the Shark PowerDetect Transformer cuts through dirt like a dorsal fin through water. As I’ve already remarked above, the bulk and weight of the Transformer really depends on which mode you use it in. In its upright form, it’s definitely on the husky side — I lift weights multiple times a week, yet I still felt the effort of dragging it round. Fortunately, its two-axis joint makes it pretty easy to maneuver around furniture and once you strip it back to its stick or handheld forms, it’s considerably easier to wield. Keen to really put the PowerDetect Transformer through its paces, I not only vacuumed my house top to bottom but conducted our full battery of standardized tests. First off, I sprinkled the contents of a teabag on a range of different flooring types to simulate the finer dust the Transformer would have to tackle. On my laminate flooring, the Transformer scarfed down those loose leaves in a single pass — even when repeating this test on my medium-pile carpet, the vacuum cleaner didn’t leave a single scrap behind. Wanting to see how it fared with more substantial debris, I tried this same test with a small quantity of lentils. Once again, on a hard floor, the Shark snorted up every single pulse without hesitation. Admittedly, when I tried this out on carpet, it left behind three lentils out of about 50. But with a single swipe backward, its automatic direction sensing flipped the direction of its suction and it wolfed them down without issue. Even trickier debris like pet hair didn’t seem to faze it. Trying it out on a ball of fuzz from my cat’s brush, the vacuum wolfed it down like cotton candy. I even put it to work on the cat’s favorite chair — which was so disgustingly furry that our previous vacuum cleaner had threatened to take industrial action — and yet Shark’s anti-hair wrap tool cut through it easily. And despite going up against upholstery more covered in hair than Hugh Jackman, it lived up to its name and didn’t get clogged or tangled. So, all in all, I found its suction pretty impressive. But even more noteworthy are how those smarts I mentioned above improve cleaning performance across the board. Thanks to the Transformer’s Dirt Detect feature, during normal cleaning it regularly dialled up its suction strength to tackle denser piles of dust without me having to even think about it. And its edge-of-room performance is fantastic — trying to vacuum up lentils I scattered right up to the baseboard, the vacuum’s Edge Detect feature targeted its suction to pick up every last legume in a single sweep. The Transformer’s other modes don’t offer quite as much smarts or power as the upright mode but they’re just as capable when tackling their own respective niches. The stick vacuum offers the same level of flexibility but a much lighter weight, making it the perfect tool for a quick runaround in a single room. Meanwhile, its handheld mode made short work of cleaning problem areas like the inside of my sofa and raised surfaces like my piano — without a bulky cyclone chamber attached, it felt so much more flexible than any other convertible vacuum handheld I’ve used. And once you’re done cleaning, emptying the Transformer feels like a breeze, especially compared to older vacuums. Once you’ve used the stick or handheld vacuums, all you need to do is re-attach the vacuum pod and it will automatically suck out all the dust you’ve gathered into that main chamber. Clearing out the vacuum pod itself is almost as easy. Detach it using the eject button and the dust bin and cyclone section come away, leaving the filter and vacuum components behind. Then all you need to do is open the bottom clip above the bin and it empties downward — far easier than banging it upside down against the bin till something finally dislodges. Easy to clean though the Transformer is, I still wouldn’t say this process is absolutely foolproof. One thing I noticed a couple of times when emptying it out is that occasionally hair clogs would get snagged in the airlock into the vacuum pod, meaning that long fibers would start clogging up the main cyclone. Now, both my feline and my human housemates are world champion shedders, meaning this issue might not affect you as often, but it does make me worry you could quickly lose suction if you don’t stay on top of this. One other slight drawback to the Transformer is a direct consequence of all its convenience and power: the noise. Reaching a volume of 74dB in upright mode and max volume of 82dB during its self-cleaning cycle, it hits the same rough volume as heavy traffic or a blender. While this didn’t bother the humans in my house that much, my cat HATED it — he found the noise while vacuuming upsetting enough but the automatic cleaning cycle sent him flying out of the room like he’d witnessed the Terminator itself. Turns out machines bellowing in rage without apparent human input is where he nopes out. Ongoing maintenance of the device is a lot less stressful, fortunately. Although you need to clean the pre-motor filters of both chambers every month, the hand vac’s post-motor filter only needs cleaning every six months and replacing every 2.5 years, while the upright’s post-motor filter only needs cleaning once a year and replacing every three. Occasionally, you might also need to wipe those smart sensors to ensure they continue functioning properly but, all in all, this isn’t particularly punishing. Should I buy the Shark PowerDetect Transformer? You don’t want to buy separate handheld, stick and upright vacuums While stick vacuums are super versatile and handhelds are essential for vacuuming upholstery and raised surfaces, neither has the capacity and suction of a full upright. The PowerDetect Transformer gives you the benefit of all three in one package. You want smart suction for every surface The Shark’s auto-detect features mean it automatically tailors its suction power depending on the surface you’re vacuuming, how much dirt it detects, the direction it’s moving and even when you’re vacuuming room edges. Given it lacks a battery, you’ll always have to use the PowerDetect Transformer hooked up to a socket. Its 8m cable will still give you a lot of range though. Maxing out at 82dB during its cleaning cycle, this vacuum cleaner is not for the faint of heart. If you’re worried about upsetting your neighbours with your midnight vacuuming, this one might not be for you. Shark PowerDetect Transformer review: also consider If you want all of the Transformer’s fancy PowerDetect features but aren’t bothered about its larger capacity, the 0.7L Shark PowerDetect Cordless Stick Vacuum is a great alternative. Yes, it comes in at roughly the same price — $429.99 / £499.99 / AU$849.99 — but as its moniker implies, it also eschews wires, making it the perfect choice for anyone who wants a super-smart, lightweight vacuum that can tackle dirt pretty much anywhere. Read our full Shark PowerDetect Cordless Stick Vacuum review. There’s a reason that the Dyson Gen5detect is our premium pick for best vacuum cleaner. Yes, part of that reason is its $949.99 / £769.99 / AU$1,549 price tag. But it’s also because of its superb suction, fantastic smart features and great battery life. Aside from capacity, the only area that the Shark PowerDetect Transformer has it beat is in vacuuming the edges of rooms, but otherwise if you’re looking for the best deluxe dirt-sucker out there the Dyson Gen5detect is likely it. Read our full Dyson Gen5detect review. How I tested the Shark PowerDetect Transformer - Tried it out on a range of flooring and with different materials I tested the Shark PowerDetect Transformer over a period of several weeks. To test its general suction, I scattered loose tea and lentils over hard floor and carpet to simulate how it would handle dust and larger debris and see how many passes it would take to suction them up. I also scattered both of these items along the edge of the room to see how well the Shark would maintain suction at the edges. On top of this, I used it to clean my whole house several times, as well as trying it out in a few specific scenarios. I tested how well it sucked up shed fur from my pet cat, as well as trying its HairPro Self-Cleaning Pet Power brush on upholstery and on the stairs to see how it removed built up hair from soft furnishings. Finally, I used a sound level meter to record how loud it was in use, recording its max volume in both upright mode and during self cleaning. I’ve been testing tech and gadgets for around 10 years, as well as editing reviews of smart home gear and appliances. When it comes to first-hand experience, I’ve tested an array of small appliances for TechRadar, including fans and coffee machines. You’ll also be pleased to hear I’m no stranger to vacuuming — otherwise, after 20 years of adulthood, the quantity of dust in my home would be approaching the level of an Egyptian tomb.

item.title: REVIEW: Corsair Voxara review: the right specs for a gamer, but a long way off ‘studio grade’
item.description:
Source: Latest from TechRadar US in News
Great sound out of the box with plosives and esses dulled, the Corsair Voxara is tuned to broadcast your voice in full-bodied detail, although noise cancellation requires software installation. Desk knocks carrying through the stand is a teething issue that will hopefully be ironed out in the next iteration, but to really compete, it needs an XLR input as well as USB-C. - -Installing Elgato Wave Link is required to access some near-mandatory features like noise cancellation Why you can trust TechRadar We spend hours testing every product or service we review, so you can be sure you're buying the best. Find out more about how we test. Corsair enters the microphones for streaming and wider mic market with this RGB-laden Voxara condenser model, a well-judged combination of specs and features for the price. If you’re looking specifically for a gaming or streaming mic and willing to pay a premium for audio quality and looks, the Voxara ticks the most important boxes. But it also makes some lofty marketing claims that aren’t relevant or helpful if you’re just trying to figure out if it’s worth the cash. For example, the 25mm capsule this mic’s built around can capture enough nuance from your voice to record and broadcast rich, well-rounded audio, while hardware and software team up to suppress esses and plosives. However, the maximum 192KHz sample rate simply isn’t relevant to most users, and it definitely doesn’t make this USB-C model a studio-grade piece of audio equipment. It’s worth knowing that to get the best sound, you’ll need to download Elgato’s Wave Link software. It’s a powerful app with a nice, clean UI, and the AI-driven Voice Focus feature is very effective at noise cancellation. Not everyone wants to have to install additional software, though, so if you want plug-and-play performance, this is a big caveat. The mic housing’s built to a high standard and the circuitry seems to be top-notch too: there’s almost no unwanted noise when you use the tap-to-mute function at the head of the housing, and the 3.5mm monitoring input runs at a sensible output range with no crackle or distortion. So you’re getting strong vocal recording, easy controls, and a pretty intuitive digital display on the mic’s front, too. These are the big selling points here, along with the visual design. But if you want a subtler look that takes its design cues from pro audio, or a mic that really can claim to offer studio-grade functionality at a similar price, you need to look further afield at options like the Shure M7+ and Rode PodMic USB. - List price: $199.99 / £159.99 / AU$329 - Decent feature set and device compatibility for the price - XLR + USB mics available in the same price bracket It might not be specced to topple all rivals, but this debut model from Corsair nonetheless offers solid value for money for the build quality, Elgato software features, and crisp sound it delivers. Available now for PC, Mac, PlayStation 5 and Nintendo Switch, it’s got a broad enough compatibility list to be your battlestation mic – just as long as that battlestation doesn’t feature an Xbox. It’s priced in a similar range to one of our favourite mics, the SteelSeries Alias, and well under Razer’s Seiren V3 Pro, which at $249.99/£249.99 represents the upper end of the gaming mic market. However, what’s hurting the overall value proposition is that lone USB-C connectivity. With Rode’s PodMic USB offering XLR and USB connections and now available for around the same price, you’d need to really like that RGB display on the Voxara. Is the Voxara well-designed? For gamers who want no-fuss, clear comms and an object on their desk that looks part of a traditional gaming setup, the answer is yes. It’s a familiar condenser design with a single cardioid polar pattern, a tap-to-mute button on top, and a scroll wheel on the bottom third, which can be used to adjust the mic, monitoring, and audio mix levels by clicking the wheel to toggle between those parameters. Finally, there’s an RGB mode cycle knob at the rear, which does what you’d expect. To help you keep track of what you’re adjusting and make a note of your settings, there’s a digital display just below the RGB capsule shield. Bonus points go to Corsair for making this display automatically flip depending on whether the mic’s pointed up or down (if you’re using the supplied desk stand or a boom arm, for example). That’s a bit of forethought that keeps things simple to dial in, whatever your current setup. Personally, I’d rather the RGB lighting wasn’t there at all, but I have to concede that it comes down to personal taste. I will say this much: given the peripheral market’s move away from copious RGB zones on mice, keyboards, and headsets lately, I wonder how quickly this model will look dated. I digress. There are three lighting modes available: a solid colour mode, a multicolor effects mode, and a level meter that responds to the audio source. While they’re fun to play around with and customise when you first get the mic, when it comes to using the Voxara in real-world situations, I found two of these three modes distracting and fell back on solid colour mode. When you’re concentrating on what’s happening onscreen, you really don’t want something so close to your face to be constantly changing the lighting conditions. And if you’re recording a podcast with a video element, the level meter in particular is an unwelcome distraction that pulls your attention away from what the hosts are saying. One area I do find the lighting useful is when muting or unmuting the mic. There’s a ring running around the tap-to-mute surface that changes colour when you tap it, and it’s very handy to know at a glance if the mic’s hot or not. Particularly if you’ve been muted for a while and lost track. All of the cosmetic-focused lighting is optional and customisable, so I’m not considering my negative experience with it a dealbreaker. But keep in mind that you’re paying a premium for that RGB. You need to be really sure that you’ll use and enjoy that functionality before shelling out; otherwise, there are non-RGB mics with great sound and better connectivity available. As you’d expect from Corsair, the finish quality of the mic housing, shock mount, and stand is all immaculate and conveys the premium price positioning. The stand holds your mic precisely where you position it, and cable management is fairly easy with a hollowed-out vertical stand that the USB-C cable can thread through. However, the stand doesn’t perform well against accidental desk knocks, so if you’re recording or streaming yourself, you’d better factor in the cost of a boom arm as well. If your broadcasting ambitions begin and end with clear callouts in Counter-Strike or Valorant, though, this shouldn’t become a problem. - Noise cancellation requires Elgato software I’m very impressed by how polished and usable this mic sounds without any tweaking. There’s no need for an additional pop shield on the Voxara, since it’s tuned to suppress esses and P sounds for a consistent and broadcast-ready sound. And that, of course, is the most important thing about any mic, whether it’s marketed to gamers or anyone else. But as someone who’s worked with plenty of studio mics, I’m always very aware there’s a significant distinction between ‘good gaming mic’ and ‘good studio mic’. Let’s start with the 25mm capsule. As with headphone drivers, bigger doesn’t always mean better in this category by default, but a large capsule of sufficient build quality is capable of capturing a wider range of frequencies and subharmonics in lots of detail. Right out of the box, if you record yourself speaking into the Voxara and listen back to the audio at any bitrate, you can hear that detail. For podcasting and Twitch streaming, it lends clarity and polish to your content. For in-game playcalling, it’s downright overkill. So big points to Corsair for getting that right. But I have to take the marketing literature to task for selling this mic as ‘studio-grade’. It’s written in huge lettering on the product page, mentioned in the reviewer’s guide, and it’s simply not accurate. The fact that this mic doesn’t have an analog input option makes it a non-starter as a studio kit. True broadcast quality requires that you keep full control of latency, preamp settings, gain amplification, and analog-to-digital signal conversion to retain as much fidelity and flexibility as possible. A USB mic builds all those elements into its internal circuitry, which makes it much simpler to use. And that’s the compromise. You don’t need a separate preamp and mixer to get a usable signal from a USB mic, and most gamers don’t have that studio equipment lying around, so gaming mics usually feature USB inputs. But there’s an implicit tradeoff to that convenience in fidelity. It isn’t night and day, but it’s there. So the fact that this mic can technically record at 192Hz doesn’t mean it can go toe-to-toe with a Neumann U87 Ai. XLR also makes simultaneous audio source recording far easier. You can run as many mics into a mixing desk as your desk inputs and DAW allow, but capturing multiple USB sources in real-time is a massive headache by comparison. Therefore, if you’re browsing the USB gaming mic market and see any product page copy talking about ‘studio quality’, go ahead and translate it to what the manufacturer really means, which is ‘sounds pretty good’. With that point addressed, the Voxara’s sound quality is more than pretty good. And you can make it even more polished with Elgato’s excellent Wave Link software. This is a double-edged sword – it’s a well-designed and user-friendly app that packs tons of functionality into a clean shell, and it can also function as a gateway into professional DAWs. There are those – myself included – who prefer not to have to download software to use their peripherals, though, so I’m in a quandary about this one. One feature in particular that’s got me conflicted is Voice Focus, an AI-powered noise suppressor that works very well indeed. On the one hand, I love that I have access to it, and on the other, I resent that it isn’t being handled automatically by the mic’s DSP. I find it easy to forgive minor grievances like that when I hear how smooth and listenable the vocal recordings are, though. It’s not easy to bring a new mic to market, and Corsair has made a lot of shrewd judgments in order to make this such a compelling option. It’s spent big on construction materials and finish quality, as it always does across any product category, teamed up with Elgato to pool some vital knowledge, and used a 25mm capsule that distinguishes itself as soon as you plug it in. That’s an impressive debut. I’m not moved to disconnect my preferred mics just yet, but I can easily envision that Corsair’s future models will give them stiff competition. Should I buy the Corsair Voxara? Buy it if... The combination of on-mic controls and Elgato Wave Link options makes this mic easy to dial in a usable setting and to adjust on the fly. Xbox is the only major platform the Voxara doesn’t support, making it a great option for hot-swapping between devices in your battlestation. …In both the literal and cringey millennial slang senses of the word, but mainly the former. This is designed to blend into a setup rich with RGB-infused peripherals. Don't buy it if... You want a mic that can handle studio tasks Without an XLR input, this mic’s usage is limited to in-game comms and streaming, making that max 192Hz sample rate all but irrelevant in most usage cases. You’re going to turn the RGB off as soon as you unbox it Gamer-focused features like the customisable RGB zone are big contributors to this model’s overall premium pricing, so don’t spend for it if you don’t intend to make full use of it. You also don’t have the budget for a good boom arm Sadly, the attractive-looking stand is susceptible to picking up desk knocks, so if you’re recording podcasts or the like, you’ll really need a good boom arm to cut that noise out. Also consider... Is Corsair’s Voxara not calling out to you? Try these alternatives. We’re big fans of how this mic looks and performs, and it’s particularly easy to get great sound right out of the box, although SteelSeries’ Sonar software does offer further tweaking. For more information, check out our full SteelSeries Alias review If you want to take the idea of speccing a microphone to a gamer’s specific needs to the extreme, and you want an XLR input thrown in too, Razer’s pricey but impressive flagship mic has you covered. For more information, check out our full Razer Seiren V3 Pro review - 20-30 hours tested across in-game comms and recording - Discord chat, in-game voice channels, Ableton recording, and Riverside podcast recording app tested - .WAV recordings contrasted and compared between mic models The first and most informal test for any gaming mic is the ‘How’s that sound?’ when you enter the Discord voice channel. Getting your friends’ feedback is an important piece of the puzzle, since they’re used to hearing your regular equipment and environment. If you sound clearer or richer with the new mic plugged in, they’ll hear it before you do. That’s part of my standardised testing for any mic, including this Voxara. But I also run the mic directly into a DAW — Ableton Live in my case — and record a dry signal featuring a few minutes of speech. That lets me compare how the mic sounds with other models I’ve tested and identify the differences. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 was released during the period I tested this mic, and its DMZ mode gave me a great environment for in-game comms. Most of the time those comms amounted to confused chatter about how to do the objective, but valuable testing time nonetheless. Promise.

item.title: REVIEW: TeamGroup GA Pro 2TB SSD Review: A faltering attempt at a mid-range PCIe 5.0 SSD
item.description:
Source: Latest from Tom's Hardware
The TeamGroup GA Pro is a drive that mostly misses. While it has relatively good points at QD8 and acceptable steady-state write speed, overall performance is very low with this inefficient, hot-running drive. Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test. Every once in a while we get a drive that comes across our desk that stands out, for good or for bad. The TeamGroup GA Pro falls into the latter category, enough so that we re-checked our results and contacted the company. We’ve managed to mostly sort out what’s going on and, while this is not the worst drive around, it has enough problems that we would generally not recommend it except if it's on steep sale. TeamGroup’s array of storage offerings knows no bounds: if there’s a niche to cover, it makes an attempt. The GA Pro feels like such a try, although we’re not completely sure where it fits into the mix. The company is still working to iron out the bugs, if it can, but the technology is old enough that we wouldn’t hold our breath. On paper, it’s a PCIe 5.0 drive with DRAM that should beat any PCIe 4.0 SSD, but we found it struggles to live up to its own class of drive. Bright points are few and far between, but at least we can say it’s not the worst drive we’ve seen. The edges are just rougher than usual. The TeamGroup GA Pro is available in 1TB, 2TB, 4TB, and 8TB capacities, although we only have the 2TB showing up at $331.99 at retail right now. The 8TB will probably be hard to find at this point. The drive is rated for up to 10,000 / 8,500 MB/s for sequential reads and writes, with no IOPS rating, although a drive like this can achieve 1 million or more. It has the standard five-year warranty with up to 600 TB of writes per TB of capacity. TeamGroup GA Pro Software and Accessories TeamGroup has a number of downloads available for this range of drives, which is better than nothing. They do maintain firmware for their drives, and we made sure our test sample had the newest revision, 050g05E7. Also available is the SSD S.M.A.R.T. TOOL, which is their SSD toolbox with basic functions, such as health monitoring. For backup and cloning on Windows, we continue to recommend MultiDrive, which continues to be updated based on user feedback. The good news is, the GA Pro has a graphene heat-spreading label. The bad news is, it’s insufficient to cool this drive. In most cases, you will want a heatsink on this. You can use a heatsink with the label in place, but you will have better luck if it’s removed. We are fond of graphene labels as they can be surprisingly effective, but it’s just not enough here. Then we have the label which, with the 3.3V / 2.5A rating, puts the drive at a very optimistic 8.25W. We measured over 12.5W peak in our testing below. We can’t go by reported power states, as these top off at 3.50 W. Since we can’t rely on that, we can’t say for sure what even the expected enter/exit latencies are, relevant given TeamGroup’s claims about the drive, which we’ll get to later. The drive is otherwise double-sided with a controller, two DRAM packages, and four NAND flash packages. The SSD controller is InnoGrit’s IG5666, the company’s answer to the Phison E26 high-end PCIe 5.0 champion. We have better controllers in that segment now, like the E28 and SMI’s SM2508, but even at the time of release, the IG5666 was not very popular. Both the E26 and IG5666 run very hot due to using an older process node, and newer flash wasn’t available yet to more easily reach the bus speeds needed. The GA Pro is not running full-out but, to be honest, that doesn’t help much. Phison put a lot of work into getting the E26 up to full speed in steps, and even the base 10 GB/s ones run toasty. The drive does have the right amount of DDR4, 2GB, for this amount of flash. No problems there. The flash also looks to be YMTC’s 232-layer TLC, which is also perfectly fine. The controller is the weak spot here and, as we’ll find out, its firmware really keeps the GA Pro from reaching its full potential, even with its bandwidth cap.
