While we’re on the subject of kickstands, here’s the one I’m buying this week. Peak Design makes good stuff, and I frequently find that I need extra juice at exactly the moment I want to watch something on a plane or train. This one’s going right into my backpack and probably never coming out. - The Bambu Lab H3C. I am dangerously close to becoming a 3D Printer Dude. At $2,500, this one’s a little steep for my wallet, but I think my colleague Sean Hollister is right that this is what the future of 3D printing looks like. Simpler, more foolproof, easy enough even for a goofus like me to make some pretty cool stuff. - “Ranking the world’s most popular pens for journaling.” I know we all love a good pen — and Peter McKinnon does an excellent job of breaking down a few dozen supposedly good pens to see which ones really hold up. I bought more than one pen after watching this. - Instagram Edits for Mac. Oh, great, just as I was finally getting good at CapCut! I like the Edits mobile app a lot, and the desktop app seems to be even a little more powerful. Plus: free. This is how I finally take down Cristiano Ronaldo. - The Sony MDR-3R headphones. Respect to Sony for taking the retro headphone trend all the way to its logical conclusion and just releasing the headphones from the original Walkman. You’ll look a little like Nathan Fielder in You Can See Everything when you wear them, and $60 ain’t cheap, but there’s something so incredibly ’70s-era cool about them. - The Motorola Signature 27. This is just a pure tour de force of a smartphone spec sheet. Monster camera; brightest screen; giant battery. Also very cool to see a flagship phone with support for GrapheneOS, for the less Google-inclined among us. It’s expensive, and only shipping… someday… but I just like that phones like this exist. We talked last week about Readwise Books, the new app that’s a mix of Kindle, Goodreads, and Strava. I’m a longtime fan and user of Readwise Reader, so I wasn’t shocked that I liked the new app a lot, too. And I’ve heard from a bunch of you that you do, too! I’ve talked to Tristan Homsi, one of the Readwise cofounders, a few times over the years, and have always enjoyed hearing his thoughts about reading, apps, and digital products in general. I asked him to share his homescreen to see if I might be able to get a hint about what he’s reading and the other stuff he thinks is good. (I also asked Daniel Doyon, Readwise’s other cofounder, to share, and he didn’t respond. Daniel is dead to me.) Here’s Tristan’s homescreen, plus some info on the apps he uses and why: The phone: iPhone 13 (!).Believe it or not, I chose to buy this relatively outdated phone last year… not because it’s my favorite form factor or anything, but because it’s closer in specs to the median device our Readwise users have and helps me build a bit more user empathy with them. I’m able to catch performance regressions and bugs in Readwise that the developers on our team with Duos and Pro Maxes and such miss. Let me tell you though, iOS 26 itself does not work amazingly on an iPhone 13. Lots of lagging and janky animations. I am somewhat bought into the conspiracy theory that they make the old phones suck so you buy a new one… not so much intentionally, but rather by virtue of just making each successive iOS use more and more resources, doing fancier and fancier things. The wallpaper: My lovely wife and my cat Sophie :) The apps: Clock, Settings, Google Calendar, Camera, Google Maps, Spotify, Bay Wheels, Oura, Eight Sleep, Auto Eight, BeReal, ChatGPT, Runmeter, Strava, Readwise Highlights, Readwise Reader, Phone, Messages, Safari. Of course, I have all three Readwise apps front and center. Highlights and Reader as app icons, and Readwise Books in widget form at the top! It’s a great reminder to jump back into your current book (I’m reading Apple in China right now… speaking of Apple!) instead of scrolling twitter (on a later page), and seeing my friends currently reading really makes me want to jump in and join them :) I also am a huge fan of the somewhat-defunct social app BeReal. It had its moment in 2022, but quite a few of my friends are still on there! You post once a day, can see what your close friends around the world are doing, and most importantly can’t get sucked in for more than two minutes since it limits you to a random photo or two a day! I still post basically every day, and have almost five years of memories in there. Speaking of getting sucked in, I don’t have it pictured on my home screen, but I also have Clearspace installed, which helps me stay off of all social media. Some other apps shown on the homescreen: “auto eight” is something I vibecoded to better control my Eight Sleep mattress (lol)… Strava and Runmeter are awesome for tracking my runs… and Bay Wheels is my main mode of commute around San Francisco daily. I also asked Tristan to share a few things he’s into right now. Here’s what he sent back: - I follow some amazing niche internet blogs, which you should check out if you haven’t. I love the blog Slime Mold Time Mold, famous for their citizen science and potato-maxxing. I also love Gwern.net, Deepfates, and Dynomight… among many others! - And of course I’m always reading books. The most recent fiction series I loved was the Red Knight series — which I can only recommend if you are into dense, dark, fantasy — but man, if you are, the author is a genius. - For non-fiction, it’s hard for me to plug anything but my favorite book of all time, The Beginning of Infinity. It’s not the easiest to get through, but if you do it will likely change the way you see the world, as it did for me! Here’s what the Installer community is into this week. I want to know what you’re into right now as well! Email installer@theverge.com or message me on Signal — @davidpierce.11 — with your recommendations for anything and everything, and we’ll feature some of our favorites here every week. For even more great recommendations, check out the replies to this post on Threads and this post on Bluesky. “Finally started reading Dungeon Crawler Carl (recommend); finding the Duo to be a perfect foldable reading device. Going to have to take a break to save Princess Zelda though.” — Will “I’m playing around with CutWire’s Drift video editor (alt to CapCut) and I’m honestly shocked at how high-quality it feels.” — Kolin “A wonderful Belgian developer put together an alternative Kobo EPUB reader called Kobalt that I’ve been really enjoying. There’s even an Android app, so I also put it on my Supernote Manta to use with larger format content. So much nicer than KOReader!” — Dylan “As a mourning Arc user, I’ve been on the search for my next browser, especially one with a good mobile experience and this one is AWESOME. Lens Browser feels like what Arc Search on mobile would have become had they stuck with it. Currently only mobile for now, but it does have a Mac toolbar companion for sharing links.” — Garrett “Since Arc Search is going away, I’ve been using Lens, and it’s exactly what I’ve been wanting in a mobile browser. It’s the perfect Arc Search replacement.” — Corey “My Boox Picco literally just arrived today. So now I’m trying to churn through Fellowship of the Ring on it, plus my economics textbook.” — Lukas “I’m trying to get back to the gym, and my motivation is I can only watch a show I want to watch if I’m on the treadmill. I’m finally starting Barry. Turns out, good show!” — Ben “Well, Zelda..., but also World of Warcraft Forever, but also 007 First Light (which is letting everyone play the opening for free).” — djstarburst “Playing the Final Fantasy Resonance demo on Switch 2 while waiting for Ocarina of Time to show up at my door and having a blast. It’s all so fresh and delightful and human!” — Olof I’ve mentioned Kagi a bunch of times in this newsletter — it has been my default search engine for the last few years, and I can’t recommend it highly enough. (What if Google, but good, you know?) The challenge with Kagi is it costs $10 a month, which is a lot to ask when Google is free. But as of this week, you can now at least try it for yourself, since Kagi will give you 50 free searches before even asking you to sign up. You get 100 more when you do, even before you pay. If you search a lot, and miss what Google used to be, give Kagi a whirl. I am a very happy customer, and suspect I will be for a long time. See you next week!

item.title: REVIEW: MelGeek VIVA63 HE review: Who needs a boring keyboard anyway?
item.description:
Source: Digital Trends
“A little keyboard with a lot of game.”
- Excellent Rapid Trigger gaming performance - Premium construction and distinctive design - Smooth switches with enjoyable typing acoustics The MelGeek VIVA63 HE is a premium 63-key Hall Effect gaming keyboard that gets the competitive fundamentals right while throwing in a few features that make it genuinely fun to use. Its TTC Pro KOM HE Magneto switches, adjustable actuation, Rapid Trigger, and 8,000Hz polling rate make it an excellent companion for competitive FPS games. But it’s the responsive OLED touchscreen, distinctive transparent design, and surprisingly enjoyable typing experience that give it personality. The compact layout, wired-only connectivity, and lack of adjustable feet are disappointing at this price, though. It’s not for everyone, but gamers looking for something a little different have plenty to like here. Design and build quality: Batman would approve The VIVA63 HE makes a rather good first impression. From the moment I pulled it out of the box, the keyboard felt properly premium. Its transparent design, substantial construction, and illuminated OLED screen give it a rather distinctive appearance. But my favorite detail has to be the black keycaps with yellow Escape and Enter keys. They give the keyboard a classic Batman vibe, and I’m absolutely here for it. The rotary volume knob deserves a mention too. It looks less like a keyboard control and more like something borrowed from a fancy desktop DAC. The construction uses a combination of ABS, PC, and metal, with a gasket-mounted structure and multiple layers of internal sound dampening. There’s no noticeable flex, creaking, rattling, or poor finishing on my review unit. At approximately 890g, it also stays comfortably planted on the desk. We’ve previously reviewed the MelGeek MADE68 Ultra V2, which takes a more industrial approach with its CNC aluminum chassis and elaborate RGB lighting. The VIVA63 HE goes in a different direction, swapping that industrial aesthetic for a transparent design and an OLED-equipped control section. The 63-key layout takes some adjustment, though. For starters, coming from a 75% keyboard, I initially struggled with the smaller right Shift key. While the rest of the arrangement became comfortable within a day or two, missing dedicated productivity keys is something to consider. I wouldn’t hold that against this keyboard, though. It is, after all, a gaming-first keyboard, and it certainly behaves like one. The OLED screen and RGB lighting are showstoppers The 1.58-inch OLED touchscreen is arguably the VIVA63 HE’s biggest differentiator. MelGeek’s LumiDeck system combines the display with an infinite rotary knob and a dedicated profile-switching key. The touchscreen is responsive, and I particularly enjoyed using custom GIFs, switching profiles, and accessing secondary keyboard functions such as Delete, Page Up, and Page Down. The knob handles volume and media controls, making it more useful than a decorative piece of hardware. I did find myself leaving the screen on its default display quite often, though. So it’s safe to say that its usefulness ultimately depends on how much time someone spends customising it. Still, having these controls readily available is a nice touch. The RGB lighting is equally impressive. Per-key illumination looks gorgeous through the transparent design, while the 270-degree lightbox adds glow around the keyboard. The lighting on the right side appears particularly bright, and it looks fantastic when gaming in a dimly lit room. Typing experience: Surprisingly good outside gaming The VIVA63 HE uses TTC Pro KOM HE Magneto magnetic switches, which feel light, smooth, and consistent across the board. More importantly, they’re highly customisable, allowing users to fine-tune actuation depending on their preferences. The MCR double-shot PBT keycaps also feel premium, with a familiar OEM-like profile. They’re comfortable for extended typing, although their opaque legends mean the RGB doesn’t shine through the letters. Acoustically, the keyboard leans towards a muted character in its stock configuration. After experimenting with the settings, I found it possible to achieve a more creamy-sounding profile. It isn’t particularly thocky, but the overall typing experience is satisfying. My biggest complaint, however, is the lack of adjustable feet. MelGeek provides a fixed typing angle of approximately seven degrees, but I’d have appreciated the flexibility to elevate the keyboard further depending on my typing position. Of course, your mileage may vary, depending heavily on your setup, usual typing position, and style of typing. Gaming performance: Rapid Trigger is the real MVP This is where the VIVA63 HE really earns its gaming credentials. I used it for three to four competitive Valorant matches almost daily for close to a month, alongside sessions of Apex Legends, CS2, Control Resonant, and Cyberpunk 2077. The difference was immediately noticeable in competitive shooters. Compared with my usual 8BitDo Retro Xbox keyboard and EvoFox Ronin X75, the VIVA63 HE felt considerably more responsive and fluid. Every movement input felt crisp, particularly when changing directions during intense firefights. Much of that comes down to its Hall Effect switches and Rapid Trigger implementation. Unlike conventional mechanical switches that rely on fixed actuation and reset points, magnetic switches detect key movement using magnetic sensors. The VIVA63 HE lets users adjust actuation between 0.1mm and 3.4mm, with 0.01mm adjustment increments. Rapid Trigger can also be configured between 0.01mm and 2.5mm. In simpler terms, Rapid Trigger allows a key to reset as soon as it moves upwards by the configured distance, rather than waiting for it to cross a conventional reset point. This makes repeated inputs and quick directional changes feel more responsive. Add to that, the support for per-key customisation also means that movement keys can have different sensitivity settings from those used for regular typing. That said, just don’t blindly set everything to the lowest possible actuation. Extremely sensitive settings can register accidental inputs when fingers are resting on keys. The keyboard also supports Dynamic Keystrokes and Snap Tap, although I decided to keep my hands off the latter. Competitive games are getting increasingly serious about SOCD-assisted movement, and I wasn’t particularly interested in turning my keyboard review into a Valorant ban appeal. Rapid Trigger was already doing plenty of heavy lifting, anyway. My advice? Check your preferred game’s rules before getting adventurous with Snap Tap or similar features. What’s a fancy keyboard worth if it gets your account sent to the shadow realm, right? As for the advertised 8,000Hz polling rate and 0.125ms latency, those numbers certainly look spicy on paper. That said, I haven’t independently measured them, so I’ll leave the benchmark bragging to MelGeek. What I can say is that the VIVA63 HE delivered an absolutely excellent gaming experience throughout my testing. Unlike other keyboards that require a third-party app, the VIVA63 uses MelGeek’s Hive Web App for actuation settings, Rapid Trigger, key remapping, profiles, RGB lighting, and OLED customisation. My experience with it on Windows 11 was entirely smooth, with no crashes or configuration headaches. The keyboard also supports Windows, macOS, and Linux, although my testing was limited to Windows 11 As far as connectivity goes, that’s where things get slightly less exciting. The VIVA63 HE is wired-only, using USB-C, with no Bluetooth or 2.4GHz wireless option. But is that a big deal-breaker? Not really, at least in my opinion. See, I understand why some buyers might complain about this omission at approximately $199. Personally, though, I don’t find it particularly inconvenient. The keyboard weighs nearly 900g, so it’s hardly something I’d regularly carry around. I also keep a charging cable on my desk for my wireless keyboards anyway. Unless switching between multiple devices is important, wired connectivity on a keyboard isn’t a deal-breaker for me. Should you buy? The MelGeek VIVA63 HE gets a whole lot right. Its Hall Effect switches and Rapid Trigger make it a seriously capable gaming keyboard, while the premium build, gorgeous RGB, OLED touchscreen, and surprisingly good typing experience give it more personality than your average esports peripheral. It’s fast, flashy, and clearly doesn’t believe in blending into the background. Of course, it isn’t without a few compromises. The compact layout takes some getting used to, the fixed typing angle could use adjustable feet, and wireless connectivity is missing. What’s more, at around $199, it also goes head-to-head with the Wooting 80HE+, which offers a more practical layout and a more established software ecosystem. It’s safe to say that while Wooting might be the sensible pick for competitive purists, the MelGeek has considerably more flair. I’d recommend the VIVA63 HE to gamers who want serious Hall Effect performance without settling for another boring black rectangle on their desk. It’s premium, responsive, ridiculously good-looking, and packed with personality. Why not try? At approximately $199.99, the Wooting 80HE+ is the more conventional competitive-gaming choice. Its 80% layout retains dedicated function and arrow keys, while Wootility offers extensive per-key actuation and Rapid Trigger customisation. It also supports True 8K polling. The VIVA63 HE counters with its OLED touchscreen, distinctive transparent design, and more elaborate lighting. Want Hall Effect gaming without spending $200? The K2 HE is a compelling alternative at $129.99. It offers Gateron magnetic switches, Rapid Trigger, adjustable actuation, a 75% layout, and tri-mode connectivity with Bluetooth, 2.4GHz, and USB-C. It also has adjustable typing angles, making it a better fit for someone juggling work and gaming. That said, its 1,000Hz polling rate is lower than MelGeek’s 8,000Hz, and it misses out on the OLED touchscreen and fancy lightbox. Another excellent Hall Effect option from MelGeek, the MADE68 Ultra V2 offers a larger 65% layout, CNC aluminum construction, and spectacular 360-degree RGB lighting. It shares the brand’s gaming-first approach but skips the VIVA63’s OLED touchscreen and rotary knob. It’s worth considering if a more substantial metal chassis and additional keys are priorities. I used the MelGeek VIVA63 HE as my primary gaming keyboard for close to a month, playing three to four competitive Valorant matches almost daily. I also tested it with Apex Legends, CS2, Control Resonant, and Cyberpunk 2077, paying particular attention to movement responsiveness, Rapid Trigger, and overall input consistency. Outside gaming, I used it for everyday typing and writing, experimented with its actuation settings and sound profile, and explored the OLED touchscreen, custom GIFs, media controls, RGB lighting, and Hive web app. I also compared its everyday usability with my usual 75% keyboard and other keyboards in my setup. FAQs (Frequently Asked Questions) Is the MelGeek VIVA63 HE a Hall Effect keyboard? Yes. It uses TTC Pro KOM HE Magneto magnetic switches with adjustable actuation and Rapid Trigger. Does the MelGeek VIVA63 HE support Rapid Trigger? Yes. Rapid Trigger is adjustable between 0.01mm and 2.5mm, allowing keys to reset and register inputs with very little movement. Is the MelGeek VIVA63 HE wireless? No. It is a wired-only gaming keyboard that connects through USB-C. Is the MelGeek VIVA63 HE good for Valorant? Yes. Its Hall Effect switches, adjustable actuation, and Rapid Trigger make it particularly well-suited to competitive FPS games such as Valorant and CS2.

item.title: SALES: What does Apple One Family come with and which subscription is best for you?
item.description:
Source: Engadget
What does Apple One Family come with and which subscription is best for you? The answer comes down to how many of Apple's services you use regularly. This year, several of Apple's subscriptions saw serious price upticks, so much so that even students had to pay a bit more. Apple Music prices rose by $1 a month for individual plans and $3 for the Family plan. A few weeks later, monthly Apple TV subscriptions went up from $13 to 15, while annual ones saw a $20 total jump. If you use many Apple services, you might have looked to Apple One to bundle them and reduce the hurt from these increases. Unfortunately, the package subscription didn't get by unscathed either. The Individual tier climbed from $20 to $22 a month, though it's still cheaper than subscribing to Apple Music ($12/month) and Apple TV ($15/month) separately. While the Apple One Family plan is now $28/month, you can share it with five other people, which drastically brings down the cost per person. There's also a higher-cost shareable Premier tier at $40/month. But before you ask friends and family to group up with you, you need to figure out which of the three Apple One subscriptions is most worth your while. That mostly depends on how many Apple services you already use. Which Apple One tier makes the most sense for you? Getting the cheapest tier out of the way: Individual subscribers get Apple TV, Apple Music, Apple Arcade and 50GB of iCloud storage for $22 per month; that's about $13 less than it would be to subscribe to each one on its own. Moving on, the Family tier is a great choice if you're providing for multiple people or want to split the monthly cost with up to five other members. At $28 per month, you get a shared 200GB pool of iCloud storage, the Apple Music Family plan (which costs $20 by itself), plus Apple TV and Apple Arcade. Combined, the Family plan saves you about $17 per month, which can stretch even further if you split the bill. With six people paying their own way, each person pays less than $5/month. Unlike some family plans, Apple doesn't require everyone to live in the same household. The final step up is Apple One Premier, which offers the full suite of Apple services and $35 in monthly savings compared to joining each one individually. Along with everything included in the Family plan, you also get Apple Fitness+ ($10 per month), Apple News+ ($13/month) and 2TB of shared iCloud storage ($10 per month). On their own, these would total $75, so it's a good value at $40 per month. Before deciding, you need to narrow down what you'll use, what you won't and how much storage you need. When I was subscribed to the Individual plan, I could have skated by with the 50GB of iCloud storage, but paying an additional $13 per month for Apple News+ was a pain. Before upgrading to Premier, I was paying about $38 per month when accounting for News+ and 200GB of iCloud Storage. At that rate, switching over to upgrade to 2TB of storage was well worth it, and it even included Apple Fitness+. In case you weren't aware, every Apple subscription within Apple One is already shareable with a Family Sharing group — with the exception of Apple Music, which requires the Family plan for multi-person access. But if your family only cares about playing the best Apple Arcade games, for example, you could pay $7/month for that and make it available to your Family Sharing group. Apple One makes the most sense when you'll use everything. What if I need more iCloud storage? You can always tack on extra iCloud storage by subscribing to iCloud+, letting you max out at 14TB of storage if you get the 12TB iCloud+ plan for $60 per month alongside Apple One Premier. While you share the pool of storage, your files are not visible to other family plan members unless you so choose. If you're already subscribed to iCloud+ with a plan that has less storage than your chosen Apple One plan, the former will be canceled, keeping any stored data intact, and you'll get a pro-rated refund. Meanwhile, if your active iCloud+ plan has more storage than your Apple One tier offers, you can keep your current plan alongside the storage Apple One provides. In case you don't need all that space, you can cancel iCloud+. When you jump to Apple One, if you're subscribed to individual Apple services, don't worry about getting charged twice. You'll stop being billed for any individual services included in whichever Apple One plan you choose.

item.title: SALES: 10 useful iPad apps that could make your daily life easier
item.description:
Source: Engadget
10 useful iPad apps that could make your daily life easier Put your iPad to good use with apps for journaling, discovering art and much more. Your iPad should make every day easier. Whether you want to build new habits or improve your routines, we've rounded up apps that put the best iPads to work in your daily life. We found these by digging a bit deeper. These aren't first-party Apple apps or subscription-only Adobe staples. It's free to get started with each, though most charge for extra features, which we've noted where applicable. Our favorite apps are elegant and well-designed, taking advantage of the entire iPad display. They also keep AI to a bare minimum. There may be machine learning to help with search and transcriptions, but you won't find fake images or bogus text generators here. If you're a voracious consumer of media, you need Sofa to help keep track of it all. Start with books, TV shows and movies, then add whatever other categories you'd like. Sofa has a clean interface that grabs title images and info to give you an overview of everything you watch (or read). Sofa's tracking feature is especially useful for remembering which episodes you've seen. Mark them off as you watch them and add notes if you like, or rely on the included summaries. Sofa tracks two different series at once for free, while paid subscribers can track unlimited titles. Sofa's free tier offers all its best features without advertisements or pop-ups begging for more. If you want to fine-tune your media tracking with custom ratings that you create and smart lists that populate based on your filters, Sofa offers a subscription for $5.99 per month, $49.99 per year or $249.99 for a lifetime membership. Unless you're a professional TV critic, you'll likely be fine with the free features. Instead of Apple Notes or Google Keep, try Bear, an app for capturing thoughts. Bear has become a productivity favorite by keeping its interface deceptively simple; it's a large notepad app without a glut of buttons and menus. While it's powerful, you don't have to use advanced features you don't need. Bear is built around smooth Markdown styling and supports tags to organize your thoughts. For example, if you find yourself often complaining about your job, tag that post with #job. You can add links, tags or even to-do tasks that are easily searchable. If that sounds complicated, ignore what you don't need and you're left with an elegant, attractive note-taking and journaling app. Bear has a reasonably-priced subscription tier ($3/month or $30/year) that offers a few extra features if you're hardcore about your notes. With it, you can sync your Bear notes between devices, as well as publish your notes using HTML or ePub to use the app as a blogging tool. After a few minutes with Flipboard, you'll wonder why it isn't preloaded on every iPad. This decentralized social experience transforms the touchscreen into a magazine with a clean layout and large images. If you read a lot of news, Flipboard is the best way to stay current. The app starts by having you select from an endless list of topics to find stories. These can start as general as sports, music or science. Or by dialing down, you might find "UEFA Champions League," "blues music" or "sustainable design." If any sources arise that you don't want to see, block them. In general, the selection is great; you can follow individual authors and sites the same way you follow topics. The best part about Flipboard is that it's totally free: it doesn't make you cough up a fee for the best content, and you can sometimes find stories that are normally trapped behind a paywall. HappySpoon is an (artificially) intelligent meal planner that helps you create a menu for the week ahead following whatever ideas or guidelines you set. The app uses AI to understand plain-language requests that you make, like "I need to use up all my chicken breast, so make a bunch of different chicken recipes." Once you've created your menu, it even generates a handy shopping list sorted by grocery store aisle. I asked the app to generate "breakfasts that are simple and on-repeat, like a big batch of muffins or oatmeal to eat every day" and it did exactly that. It also understood the rule "no lunches" and left that spot blank on my weekly menu. HappySpoon automatically resizes your portions and recipes to match your eaters. You can specify adult-sized or kid-sized appetites, and it will conform: the grocery list populates with the right amounts. You don't need to use HappySpoon's AI features; in fact, they're only free for two weeks. That's enough time to get started and use the AI for help generating a variety of menus. There are plenty of other AI tools that can create recipes, but if you want to stick with HappySpoon, the fee is $5.99 per month or $49.99 per year. I found the AI tools useful at first, but after a couple of weeks, the extra AI benefits didn't seem necessary. Whatever you need to organize, MindNode is a perfect starting point. Whether it's a meeting agenda, a workout plan or your life's goals, MindNode offers a simple canvas to connect and organize thoughts. You'll find features to enhance, stylize and reorganize your finished maps. Start with the big idea in the center and then branch out. A map can grow large the more you dig in, but MindNode makes it easy to keep your idea maps looking neat. You also have the option to view your maps as a text outline instead. If this sort of mental organization appeals to you, the premium subscription may offer enough bonus features to make it worth the asking $2.99 per month or $24.99 per year. With the subscription, you get more editing tools, the ability to add photos and emoji to your nodes and some professional-strength features for teams working together. It also unlocks real-time collaboration with others so you see edits and additions as they happen. You can set each node as a task with a reminder and checklist. And Apple Intelligence will enhance the experience by offering new ideas, summarizing what it sees and similar. The AI extras aren't necessary, but are available with the premium plan. Journey is a place to store your memories, including journal entries, calendar appointments , major dates, photos, multimedia and maps of the places you've been. The more you use Journey, the more it rewards your dedication, with features that track your habits later on. The available templates are Journey's secret weapon. If you're planning a trip, for example, the travel planner template includes fields for details like your hotel address, flight information, car rental details and even a budget planner that tracks your anticipated versus actual spending. Templates include tons of other categories, from personal goal trackers to a 30-60-90 day plan for starting a new career. Once you've built a journaling habit, you're able to track your progress through Journey's graphs and statistics. If you tag each journal entry with a mood, you'll see how your feelings ebbed and flowed throughout your journaling experience. By paying $6.99 per month or $49.99 per year (or $199 for the app's lifetime), you get premium features that could be helpful if you share a journal with someone else. There's also a premium AI feature included, though thankfully it doesn't offer to write journal entries for you. Instead, you can ask "how many entries did I write last month?" or tell it to "summarize my summer vacation from 2026." Libby is your local library in app form, which should be enough to earn an immediate download. Did you know you can borrow ebooks from your library? Just register your library card with Libby — go get one if you don't have one! — and you're ready to download the glut of digital content you might not have even known your library offered. Libby handles the borrowing and serves you the book in its own ereader interface, or you can put titles on your Kindle. Libraries have limited copies even for ebook titles, and Libby lets you join a waiting list for the latest best-seller if you can't grab it right away. There are audiobooks available as well, in addition to other common library finds like periodicals, graphic novels and comic books. If you can't find the title you want, Libby has an option to send requests so your local library secures a copy. And because it's a library, there's no premium offering; just borrow books and enjoy them. If journaling seems like a chore, Day One does the grunt work for you. Every time you start an entry, it records the time and date, your location, the weather and even the phase of the moon. The app isn't shy about prompting you with topics to get your journal started. If you've wanted to start a journal but don't know where to begin, Day One is ready for you. There are several categories of prompts, including Reflection, Fitness and The Year Ahead. Under Mindfulness, you might find simple prompts like "How am I feeling right now?" or introspective questions like "How often do I observe my thoughts without judgment?" If you don't want to begin with a prompt, Day One is able to access your photos, maps and calendar to pull together a summary of your day. You can add a calendar event, the map of where you went and the photos you took there. Day One puts an emphasis on privacy, with an app-specific passcode to protect your journals. There's a setting to turn off all AI-based features if you prefer. Day One will record an unlimited number of journal entries without paying a dime, but if you want to add unlimited photos and videos, or audio recordings, you'll need to pay a subscription fee. For $49.99/year you get all that, plus interesting integration with IFTTT (If This Then That) and other markup tools. Habitify can help you build habits without being intrusive or making you do so much work that the app becomes its own "habit" to maintain. You design a habit or goal, then Habitify monitors your progress in the background as much as it can. It's the rare app that you barely need to use to get value from. You tell Habitify what you want to do and on which days you'll repeat the habit, then give it a specific goal. Habitify integrates neatly with Siri, so you often won't need to open the app to log your habit since Siri will. Siri can even update you on your progress — just ask how you're doing with your goals and Habitify will feed Siri the answer. There is a paid option for $49.99 per year, which is useful if fitness is your goal since Apple Health and Google Health integrations sit behind that paywall. You can connect Habitify to your Apple Watch or Fitbit so it knows you kept up your routine. It works with Apple Health and Google Health to gather data, with your permission. The paid option can also monitor your screen time if limits are part of your habit goals. DailyArt is for art world enthusiasts who want to go beyond the most prolific canvases and dive deeper into the lives of the artists who created them. One recent offering was a gorgeous Autumn Landscape created in 1899 by the pseudonymous Hishida Shunsō. In addition to the image, the app offers a brief history of the work and artist, with an explanation of the style it exemplifies. You can select the artist name or other links to see more artwork, or wait until tomorrow to see what DailyArt serves up next. The feature are robust, so if you have a burgeoning curiosity in the art world, this is a great way to start. It offers collections grouped by artist, artistic movement or other qualities. You'll find a collection of paintings that all depict people working with their hands or a collection of cats in art, for example. There are also quizzes and games if you want to have a bit of fun. DailyArt has an unobtrusive ad bar near the bottom of the screen, plus a premium option for $4.99 per month or $29.99 per year. Along with removing ads, this also gives you unlimited searches in a vast library of high-quality artwork, with accompanying information to build your art knowledge.

item.title: SALES: Where to get the best fish and chips in London
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel
An undercover fish and chips expert's top five 'chippies' in London Stephen Peel of The Chippy Tour is on a mission to protect the nation's traditional fish and chip shops. He's rated 260, but we convinced him to choose just five of his favourites in London. Stephen Peel has just returned from judging the 2026 English Fish and Chip Awards, where he ate 14 portions of fried fish in little more than an hour. But eating one battered fish after another is nothing new for Peel, creator of The Chippy Tour. Stephen Peel is the author of several travel and culinary books. He is a frequent participant and judge at fish and chip industry awards and events, including the 2026 Scottish Fish and Chip Awards. His incognito reviews can be found on The Chippy Tour's YouTube page. (Credit: Courtesy of The Chippy Tour) Since 2024, Peel and his wife Sue have rated more than 260 "chippies" (traditional fish and chips shops) across the UK, arriving unannounced – and sometimes sending in decoys to order – before reviewing their meals from their pickup truck. "It's about supporting our chippies, finding hidden gems that get overlooked and discovering places with great stories to tell," says Peel. It's a storied culinary tradition increasingly at risk – as of 2026, 7,210 fish and chip shops remain in the UK. "Twenty years ago, there was probably about 30,000," says Peel. "People's tastes have changed – young people have got used to having McDonald's and other things just a phone call away through Uber Eats. Fish [prices have] doubled since last year. It's sad to see people struggling. They're being pushed to diversify from traditional chippy fare into fried chicken, pizzas, kebabs." Based in Cheshire, Peel regularly visits London, believing the capital to be "important" to the nation's chippy tradition. "Tourists often see it as the epicentre of our fish and chip culture... You only get one chance to make a first impression." Visitors typically encounter fish and chips in London's gastropubs and restaurants, but the classic chippy experience is a no-frills takeaway: "There's something special about popping into a chip shop and coming out with a takeaway you can pick at on the move." Peel favours family-run, independent chippies, and appreciates that London's ever-changing demographics bring in delicious flavours from around the world. "They'll add those [international] seasonings to their batter and that makes a huge difference." Here are Peel's top five London chippies. What's the best London chippy for a variety of fresh, local fish? Brockley's Rock [in Brockley, south-east London] is a family-owned chippy established in 2011 by the lovely Karoulla family, originally from Cyprus. The shop used to be a Chinese takeaway, but has now become, in my opinion, an incredible London chippy, with an emphasis on sustainable seafood. Along with fish and chips, the shop offers several fish species. It also offers gluten-free, vegetarian and vegan options. They have pollock on there, they have bass. They have grilled fish on the menu. They'll try and get [fish] in that [doesn't come from] too far away. [Their batter] is absolutely lovely; crispy, light, not greasy at all. But something else on the menu really stood out to me: their calamari with sweet chilli and ginger dip. It's absolutely to die for! During the summer months, the shop supplies picnic blankets for customers to take to [Hilly Fields], the lovely park around the corner to enjoy their fish and chips. On the condition that they return the blankets, of course. It's a fabulous shop with fabulous people. The best traditional beef-dripping chippy? Marlow Fish Bar [in Anerley, South London] is a traditional, family-owned chippy said to have served its community since 1962. The family has Cypriot heritage, still reflected inside, along with a collection of Crystal Palace football memorabilia. It's a real old-fashioned chippy and they cook the fish to order in beef dripping (tallow). Beef dripping, once the main cooking medium nationwide, is making a real comeback, though it may not suit every tourist because of religious or dietary preferences. But I've found that people will travel many miles to enjoy [beef-dripping] fish and chips. There's only two [beef-dripping] chippies that I know of in London. They actually even do halal beef dripping now. I think there's going to be more and more as people move away from seed oils. For visitors who eat beef products, a beef-dripping chippy offers something different. Visitors can experience a bit of Britain's fish and chip heritage. The smell of the beef dripping when you walk up is unmistakable. The best retro shop? Fishcotheque [in Waterloo] is tucked beneath the railway bridge on Waterloo Road. The chippy dates to 1964 and offers a taste of tradition in a relaxed, nostalgic setting. How to eat fish and chips – the English way Fish and chips is finger food, unless you're in a restaurant. Why've you got a fork there? It's fish and chips! You've got to pick it up. If you've got a whole piece of fish, you break it in half and then you hold that half and eat it like that. The condiments and sauces are for the chips. You've got to have some vinegar on your fish and chips. There's always an argument – which comes first? Vinegar first, then the salt so it sticks to the vinegar. [But] there shouldn't really be a law. That's what makes fish and chips an easy food – there's no strict way to eat it. Just go for it! The menu includes cod, haddock, plaice, rock salmon and scampi, along with traditional favourites like pies and sometimes novelty things like deep-fried chocolate bars. There's also a dining area. They also have saveloys (smoked pork sausages) [and] battered sausage. Saveloys are a big thing in the south of England. I think that's another thing that people should try when they're in London. [Visitors won't always] be familiar with some of the foods that we do in the chip shops besides fish and chips, like the saveloy and potato scallop (battered, deep-fried slice of potato). Traditional chippies that have survived while things change around them will always have a place in my heart. The steel railway bridge almost above the chippy really sets a unique historic scene. Their fried fish is flaky, white – everything about it is just spot on. The best for homemade sides and giant portions? Joseph's Fish & Chips is a family chip shop on Tower Bridge Road, within walking distance of some of London's famous attractions. Turan Tunc opened the shop in honour of his father, [who] ran kebab shops around London for more than 50 years. [They] source fresh fish from Peterhead in Scotland, an incredibly important fishing port. [Their] potatoes usually come from Cambridgeshire, while [Tunc's] wife creates delicious mushy peas and tartare sauce, as well as homemade pickled vegetables. A great feature is a giant map where visitors can place a pin to show where they are visiting from around the world. Big portions are what this place is all about. Huge portions! But it's not cheap. You could probably split the meal between yourself and a partner. Nice thick chips and a nice light batter. It's more modern than any of the others that we've mentioned but that's not a problem – you can only have so much tradition. It's warm, welcoming, clean. [Fishers in Fulham] has an extensive traditional menu including cod and haddock, along with rock salmon and skate when available. I go for cod there, as I often do in the south of England. They serve mushy peas, curry sauce and even gravy – not usual for London. The mushy peas are quite special; thick, not over-seasoned, and not overdone with food colouring, like some. The chips are very thick yet cooked through perfectly. The cod is exactly what you want from a traditional chippy: light in colour with crispy peaks, not overly thick, and not soggy anywhere. [It's] brilliant white, with large flakes and a subtly sweet aroma, and there's plenty of it. They also offer halal sausage. The shop has a great traditional feel and look, seating inside and out, with modern furnishings. They pride themselves on having a 'secret garden' for dining in warmer weather. [It's] one of the few that encourages customers to eat in. How do you rate a proper plate of fish and chips? You don't want to smell fish – battered fish doesn't smell like fish. You might get a bit of an aroma of the sea, but not fish. And you want it to be white, not yellow. When you break open that battered fish, you [don't want to find] that thick layer of goo inside that hasn't cooked. It's got to be crisp. And when you [get to] the fish, ideally a nice thick piece, you want it to fall apart. It's got to be very moist. [The chips] are not skinny little fries. You get those at McDonald's – nobody wants to see them in a chippy. They've got to be thick, they've got to have a bit of a crispness to them. They've got to be able to cave in when you put a bit of pressure on. item.title: SALES: Best hotels in Palma, Mallorca for the best of both city living and beach bliss
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Palma is having a moment. Although, for those who know Mallorca’s capital, it has been having one for quite some time. This is a city that wears its history beautifully, where Gothic spires rise above a labyrinth of cobbled medieval streets, grand palacios conceal leafy courtyards and the Mediterranean is never far from view. But beneath its honey-coloured stone and centuries of history, Palma has a distinctly contemporary pulse. Art galleries multiply by the month, tucked between independent boutiques, vintage shops and handsome old townhouses. Along Passeig del Born, designer flagships rub shoulders with elegant cafés, while La Rambla’s flower stalls lend a wonderfully old-fashioned charm. Santa Catalina, with its bustling market, neighbourhood restaurants and lively bars, remains one of the city’s most appealing quarters, while the once-forgotten district of El Terreno is enjoying a gloriously louche renaissance. There is extraordinary shopping, a flourishing restaurant scene – both old-school cosy and Michelin starred – and an increasingly sophisticated cultural life, all wrapped up in a city that remains resolutely maritime. And unlike so many Mediterranean destinations, Palma belongs to every season. Winter brings crisp blue skies, long lunches in the sunshine and galleries without the crowds; summer stretches into balmy evenings spent wandering between tapas bars and waterfront terraces. Its hotels are every bit as compelling. There are magnificent aristocratic palaces transformed into intimate hideaways, impossibly romantic townhouses, quietly luxurious family-friendly retreats and bold contemporary design hotels. Beyond the old town, grand hillside castles overlook the bay, while glamorous seafront resorts make the Mediterranean the main event. Whether the mood calls for old-school grandeur, Scandinavian minimalism or something altogether sexier, Palma has a hotel to match. item.title: SALES: 13 best Christmas markets in Europe, from Antwerp to Málaga
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Christmas is the ultimate season of indulgence, and there are few better places for a festive culinary expedition than Europe's Christmas markets. There are some winter treats that are easy to find at markets across the continent, like hot chocolate, mulled wine, cheese fondue and sizzling sausages. As someone who loves exploring places through their traditional food, though, I always make sure to try some local Christmas delicacies wherever I go. I’m from the south of Italy, and when I go home for Christmas I can't wait to eat cullurielli, traditional fried doughnuts that can be either sweet or savoury and can only be found at this time of year, while in the UK, I’m never too far from a mince pie. Every year, without fail, we haul on our winter coats for a mooch around a Christmas market – Grinches aside, of course. We’ve got the Germans (or at least German-speaking parts of Europe) to thank for the tradition, although markets that occupied courtyards and town squares in the Late Middle Ages looked quite different from the Christmas markets in Europe we're committed to exploring today. Rich hot chocolates and steaming mulled wine in hand, exploring a market in a new European city is a joy for any travel enthusiast as the temperatures dip – there are those in Spain and southern Italy, if light jackets are preferred. Here, we round up the best Christmas markets in Europe that warrant a weekend away from the festive chaos and preparations back home. Which is Europe's largest Christmas market? Strasbourg Christmas Market in France is one of the largest in Europe, with around 300 wooden chalets spread across the city's historic centre. Dating back to 1570, it's also one of the oldest, drawing visitors for its handmade crafts, traditional Alsatian treats and festive decorations. Germany is home to several other enormous Christmas markets, including those in Stuttgart, Frankfurt and Nuremberg, although there's no universally agreed ranking of Europe's largest by number of stalls or overall size. Which is the cheapest Christmas market in Europe? Warsaw in Poland is the cheapest European destination for a Christmas market city break, with accommodation averaging £110 per person per night in December. Kraków also makes the top five, coming fifth at £131 per person per night, while Budapest and Berlin are among the more affordable options. Prices vary depending on when you travel, but these cities are worth considering if you're hoping to enjoy the festive atmosphere without spending a fortune. What is the most Christmassy town in Europe? Few places capture the magic of Christmas quite like Rothenburg ob der Tauber in Germany. With its cobbled streets, half-timbered houses and medieval walls, the Bavarian town looks like something out of a Christmas storybook even before the decorations go up. Its traditional Reiterlesmarkt Christmas market fills the old town with wooden stalls selling handmade crafts, festive decorations and seasonal treats. For something on a larger scale, Strasbourg in France, often called the Capital of Christmas, is another strong contender. Here are some more of our Christmas round-ups to enjoy:
